Lecture 6 — NEO 2026

Rocks & Minerals

From atoms to landscapes — understanding how Earth builds and recycles its solid materials.

Chapter: 7 — The Good Earth Topics: Minerals · Igneous · Sedimentary · Metamorphic · Rock Cycle Source: McGraw-Hill / Lecture Slides Ch07
1

Why Study Rocks and Minerals?

Earth scientists are essentially nature's detectives — they read the rock record to understand where we've been, what resources exist beneath our feet, and what hazards might lie ahead. Even the question "Are the rocks on Mars the same as rocks on Earth?" emerges from this spirit of inquiry.

  • Locate mineral resources — copper, gypsum, rare earth elements
  • Find fossil fuels — oil, natural gas, coal reservoirs
  • Assess natural hazards — volcanic eruptions, tsunami-triggering earthquakes
  • Understand plate tectonics — rocks record Earth's internal engine
  • Explore planetary science — rock composition reveals planetary histories

Early Theories of Rock Formation

🌊 Neptunism

18th-century idea that all rocks precipitated from or settled out of a primordial global ocean. Championed by Werner. Largely disproved but contained the seed of truth about sedimentary processes.

🔥 Plutonism

Championed by Hutton — Earth's interior heat melts and fuses rocks. This underpins our modern understanding of igneous processes and is essentially correct for that rock family.

🧱 Analogy: Brick Making Brick manufacture parallels rock formation remarkably well: raw earth materials are physically broken down, chemically altered, and thermally processed. Just like rocks, brick color depends on raw material composition (red bricks = more iron). This analogy helps demystify how "rock" is made.
2

Elements, Atoms & Chemical Bonds

The geosphere — the solid Earth — is composed of rocks and related materials. Every rock is made of minerals, every mineral is made of elements, and every element is made of atoms. Understanding this hierarchy is the bedrock (pun intended) of all rock identification.

The Atom

An atom is the smallest particle that retains the characteristics of an element. It consists of:

  • Protons & Neutrons — packed in the nucleus; protons carry positive charge
  • Electrons — surround the nucleus in an electron cloud; carry negative charge
  • Atomic Number — the number of protons; this uniquely defines each element (e.g., Neon = 10, Helium = 2)

When atoms gain or lose electrons, they become ions. Oxygen (8 protons, 10 electrons) becomes O²⁻; silicon loses 4 electrons to become Si⁴⁺. These charged ions then bond together to form minerals.

Types of Chemical Bonds

⚡ Ionic Bonds (Velcro analogy)

Formed by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Relatively weaker. Example: Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → Halite (rock salt, NaCl). Minerals with ionic bonds tend to be more soluble and less resistant at Earth's surface.

🔗 Covalent Bonds (Rope analogy)

Formed by shared electrons between atoms. Stronger — produces more resistant minerals. Example: H₂O (water), diamond. Silicate minerals use a mix of ionic and covalent bonding, making them the dominant and most durable mineral group.

The Silica Tetrahedron — Earth's Master Building Block

Silicon and oxygen are the two most common elements in Earth's crust. Four oxygen atoms bond covalently around one silicon atom to form a silica tetrahedron (SiO₄) — carrying a net charge of 4−. This unit then bonds ionically with other elements (Ca, Na, K, Mg, Fe, Al) to form the vast family of silicate minerals.

  • Low silica content → simple structures → olivine, amphibole
  • High silica content → complex 3D networks → quartz, feldspar
📊 8 Elements = 98% of the Crust Oxygen, Silicon, Aluminum, Iron, Calcium, Sodium, Potassium, and Magnesium collectively make up roughly 98% of continental crust by mass. Everything else is a trace element. This is why the silicate mineral group dominates all rock types on Earth.
3

Minerals: Identification & Properties

A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid of one or more elements with a definite chemical composition and an orderly internal arrangement of atoms. There are roughly 4,000 known minerals, but only about 20 are truly common in rocks.

Key Identification Properties

Geologists use a systematic toolkit of physical properties to identify minerals in the field and laboratory. Think of it as a "mineral fingerprint":

Crystal Form

The external shape produced by the internal atomic structure. Common forms include prisms, pyramids, needles, cubes, and sheets. Example: calcite forms pyramidal crystals; tourmaline grows as needles.

Cleavage

The tendency to break along flat planes of weakness (across weaker ionic bonds). Mica: 1 perfect cleavage plane (splits into sheets). Feldspar: 2 cleavage planes at 90°. Amphibole: 2 cleavage planes NOT at 90° (≈60°/120° — a key distinction from pyroxene's 90° cleavage).

Hardness

Ranked on Mohs Scale (1 = talc; 10 = diamond). Harder minerals scratch softer ones. Softer minerals weather faster. Quartz (hardness 7) is therefore very resistant and accumulates on beaches and in sandstone.

Color

Dark minerals (black/dark green/brown) = olivine, amphibole, pyroxene, biotite → iron- and magnesium-rich. Light minerals (white/gray/pink) = quartz, feldspar, muscovite, calcite. Caution: some minerals (like fluorite) show many colors due to impurities.

Streak

The color of the powdered mineral when scratched on unglazed porcelain. More consistent than surface color. Hematite has a red-brown streak regardless of surface color.

Luster

How light reflects off the mineral surface. Metallic (iron pyrite, galena) vs. non-metallic (glassy/vitreous for quartz; pearly for mica; waxy for serpentine).

Diaphaneity

Transparency to light: transparent (clear quartz), translucent (calcite), or opaque (pyrite, magnetite).

⚠️ Exam Trap: Amphibole vs. Pyroxene Cleavage Both are dark, chain silicates — but amphibole cleaves at ~60°/120° while pyroxene cleaves at ~90°. In hand specimens, look for the angle between cleavage faces as the key diagnostic feature.
4

Igneous Rocks

Igneous rocks form from the cooling and solidification of magma (molten rock below surface) or lava (molten rock at the surface). They are classified by two key properties: texture (crystal size) and composition (silica content = color).

Origin: Volcanic vs. Plutonic

🌋 Volcanic (Extrusive) Rocks

Magma erupts onto Earth's surface as lava. Rapid cooling → microscopic or glassy crystals. Produces fine-grained (aphanitic) or glassy textures. Examples: Basalt, Rhyolite, Obsidian, Pumice, Scoria.

⛰️ Plutonic (Intrusive) Rocks

Magma cools slowly deep underground in bodies called plutons (batholiths, stocks, sills, dikes, laccoliths). Slow cooling → large visible crystals. Produces coarse-grained (phaneritic) textures. Examples: Granite, Gabbro, Diorite, Peridotite.

Texture Classification

Texture NameCrystal SizeCooling RateExample Rocks
GlassyNo crystalsExtremely rapid (surface quench)Obsidian
AphaniticMicroscopic (<0.5 mm)Rapid (volcanic)Basalt, Rhyolite, Andesite
PhaneriticVisible (>0.5 mm)Slow (plutonic)Granite, Gabbro, Diorite
PegmatiticVery large (>3 cm)Very slow + water-rich magmaPegmatitic Granite
PorphyriticMixed (large + small)Two-stage (slow then fast)Porphyritic Granite/Basalt
VesicularBubble holesRapid with gas escapePumice, Scoria
PyroclasticFragments <2mmExplosive ejectionVolcanic Tuff

Composition Classification: Mafic vs. Felsic

The silica content of magma controls both the color and viscosity of the resulting rock:

  • Felsic (high silica, 65–75% SiO₂): Light-colored. Rich in quartz and K-feldspar. High viscosity → magma tends to stay underground → plutonic. Examples: Granite (plutonic), Rhyolite (volcanic).
  • Intermediate (andesitic, ~60% SiO₂): Medium gray. Rich in plagioclase feldspar. Examples: Diorite (plutonic), Andesite (volcanic).
  • Mafic (low silica, 45–55% SiO₂): Dark-colored. Rich in amphibole, pyroxene, olivine. Low viscosity → lava flows easily. Examples: Gabbro (plutonic), Basalt (volcanic). Forms oceanic crust.
  • Ultramafic (<45% SiO₂): Very dark/black. Almost entirely olivine and pyroxene. Rare at surface. Example: Peridotite — makes up Earth's mantle.
Figure 4.1 — Igneous rock classification chart. Cross-reference color index (% mafic minerals), mineral composition, and texture to identify the rock name. Note the felsic–mafic gradient and intrusive–extrusive distinction. (Source: Lecture slides, Ch. 7)

Three Magma Types and Their Sources

  • Basaltic magma — generated by partial melting of the asthenosphere (upper mantle). Low silica, low viscosity. Reaches surface easily → basalt lava flows (e.g., Hawaii).
  • Andesitic magma — generated by partial melting of mantle rocks with added water (subduction zones). Intermediate silica. Produces andesite volcanoes (e.g., Cascades, Andes).
  • Rhyolitic magma — generated by melting of continental crust. High silica, very viscous. Often stays underground → granite batholiths (e.g., Sierra Nevada, California).

    • Bowen's Reaction Series

    As magma cools from ~1400°C to ~600°C, minerals crystallize in a predictable sequence. This is called Bowen's Reaction Series. Early-forming minerals (olivine at high T) are mafic; late-forming minerals (quartz at low T) are felsic. This explains why different magma compositions produce different mineral assemblages.

    Figure 4.2 — Bowen's Reaction Series. Minerals crystallize in sequence as magma cools. Olivine forms first at highest temperatures; quartz and muscovite last. This explains the consistent mineral assemblages found in different igneous rock types. (Source: Lecture slides, Ch. 7)
    🔑 Key Relationship: Texture + Composition = Rock Name A dark, fine-grained rock = basalt (volcanic, mafic). A light, coarse-grained rock = granite (plutonic, felsic). A porphyritic dark rock = porphyritic basalt (two-stage cooling). Practice this matrix until it's automatic — it's a core practical skill for rock identification.
    5

    Sedimentary Rocks

    Sedimentary rocks form at or near Earth's surface through the collection and lithification of material derived from pre-existing rocks, organic matter, or chemical precipitation. They characteristically form horizontal layers (beds), with the oldest beds at the bottom — a principle called the Law of Superposition.

    There are three main types, categorized by origin: Clastic, Chemical, and Biochemical.

    Type 1: Clastic Sedimentary Rocks

    Formed from fragments (clasts) of pre-existing rocks and minerals. The most common sedimentary rock type. Formation follows three stages:

  • Generation (Weathering) — Physical and chemical breakdown of rock at Earth's surface produces sediment particles. Classified by grain size: clay → silt → sand → gravel (increasing size).
  • Transportation (Erosion) — Sediment is moved from source by streams, wind, or glaciers. Larger grains require higher transport velocity. Sorting occurs: beaches accumulate sand-sized grains; river channels separate gravel (flood) from sand (moderate flow) from mud (slow flow).
  • Lithification (Deposition + Compaction + Cementation) — When transport medium slows, grains deposit (largest first). Over time, overlying weight compacts sediment; minerals precipitate from pore water to cement grains together, forming solid rock.
    • Rock NameGrain SizeCompositionEnvironment Clue
    Mudstone / ShaleClay + Silt (<0.06 mm)Clay mineralsStill water: lakes, deep sea, floodplains
    SandstoneSand (0.06–2 mm)Quartz dominantBeaches, river bars, desert dunes
    ConglomerateGravel (>2 mm)Rounded rock fragmentsRiver channels, alluvial fans

    Type 2: Chemical Sedimentary Rocks

    Form when dissolved minerals precipitate (crystallize) from water as physical conditions change — most commonly through evaporation. Commonly called evaporites because most form in shallow, restricted marine or lake settings where water evaporates.

    • Example: Halite (rock salt, NaCl) — precipitated from evaporating seawater or lake brine (e.g., ancient Lake Bonneville, Utah).
    • Example: Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) — also an evaporite; used in drywall and plaster.
    • Example: Travertine/Limestone — CaCO₃ precipitated from fresh spring water or hot springs.

    Type 3: Biochemical Sedimentary Rocks

    Bridge the biosphere and geosphere — formed by living organisms extracting minerals from solution, or from accumulated remains of dead organisms.

    • Limestone (coral reef type) — Coral organisms extract calcite (CaCO₃) from seawater to build tropical reef structures. Indicates ancient warm, shallow seas.
    • Coquina — Limestone built from broken shell fragments cemented together.
    • Chalk — Limestone formed from billions of coccoliths (round calcite plates of microscopic coccolithophore algae). Indicates cold marine conditions.
    • Coal — Carbon-rich rock from compacted, buried plant remains. Indicates ancient swampy forests.
    💡 Sedimentary Rocks as Environmental Archives Every sedimentary rock is a fossil environment. Grain size tells you energy; composition tells you climate; fossils tell you biology. A coarse sandstone layer inside a shale sequence means a high-energy event (storm, flood) interrupted quiet deposition. Reading this history is called stratigraphy — one of geology's most powerful tools.

    Fossil Fuels and Sedimentary Rocks

    The world's energy supply is embedded in sedimentary sequences. Oil and natural gas form from buried organic-rich sediments chemically altered by temperatures of 50–100°C over millions of years. Coal forms from buried plant material under increasing burial depth and heat (lignite → bituminous → anthracite — each grade reflecting greater maturity).

    6

    Metamorphic Rocks

    Metamorphism means "change of form." It refers to changes in the mineral composition and/or texture of a solid rock due to increased temperature and/or pressure — without the rock actually melting. The original rock is called the protolith (parent rock).

    📌 Temperature Range Metamorphism operates roughly between 200°C (onset of significant mineral reactions) and ~1100°C (melting point, beyond which you get magma). These conditions occur deep in the crust or near magma chambers.

    Changes During Metamorphism

    • Phase Changes — New minerals grow from existing elements but with a different crystal structure (e.g., graphite → diamond under extreme pressure; calcite → new interlocking calcite texture in marble).
    • Recrystallization — Mineral type stays the same but grain size and shape change (e.g., fine-grained calcite in limestone → coarse interlocking calcite in marble).
    • Foliation — Platy minerals (mica, chlorite) reorient perpendicular to the direction of pressure, creating parallel layers. This is the defining texture of most metamorphic rocks.

    Two Types of Metamorphism

    1. Contact Metamorphism

    Driven primarily by heat near a magma chamber (intrusion). The "baking" effect. Affects a relatively small zone around the intrusion (aureole). Creates non-foliated rocks because pressure is not directional.

    Analogy: bread → toast (heat only, no squeezing)

    Examples: Marble (from limestone); Quartzite (from sandstone); Hornfels (from shale, fine-grained).

    2. Regional Metamorphism

    Driven by heat + directional pressure during mountain-building (plate tectonics). Affects large regions. Creates strongly foliated rocks because minerals grow perpendicular to the compressional stress direction.

    Analogy: squeezing clay — it flattens and layers form perpendicular to squeeze direction

    Examples: Slate, Phyllite, Schist, Gneiss (a progressive metamorphic sequence from shale).

    Foliated Metamorphic Rocks — A Progressive Sequence

    As a shale (mud protolith) experiences progressively higher temperatures and pressures, it transforms through a predictable sequence:

    Rock NameGradeGrain SizeKey FeaturesProtolith
    SlateVery LowMicroscopicSplits into flat sheets; dull luster; fine layersShale
    PhylliteLowFineSilky/waxy sheen; crenulated surfaces; layers visible naked eyeShale/Slate
    SchistMediumCoarseSparkly; prominent mica/biotite layers; wavy foliation (schistosity)Phyllite
    GneissHighCoarseAlternating light (feldspar/quartz) and dark (amphibole/biotite) bands; banded foliationGranite or Schist

    Non-Foliated Metamorphic Rocks

    When the protolith lacks platy minerals (no mica, no chlorite), pressure cannot produce foliation. These rocks recrystallize into interlocking grain textures:

    • Marble — interlocking calcite or dolomite crystals. Protolith: limestone or dolostone. Used in sculpture and architecture.
    • Quartzite — interlocking quartz crystals. Protolith: sandstone. Extremely hard and resistant to weathering.
    Figure 6.1 — Metamorphic rock classification by texture and composition. Foliated rocks progress from low-grade (slate, chlorite-rich) to high-grade (gneiss, amphibole/pyroxene). Non-foliated rocks (quartzite, marble) lack platy minerals. (Source: Lecture slides, Ch. 7)
    7

    The Rock Cycle

    The rock cycle is the grand unifying concept of petrology (rock science): it shows how igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks are interconnected, and how any rock can be transformed into any other rock type given the right conditions and sufficient time.

    Figure 7.1 — The Rock Cycle. Arrows represent processes: melting/crystallization (igneous), weathering/transport/lithification (sedimentary), heat & pressure (metamorphic), and melting (back to magma). No rock type is permanent — all are recycled over geological time. (Source: Lecture slides, Ch. 7)

    Key Processes in the Rock Cycle

    ProcessWhat HappensRock Outcome
    Cooling & SolidificationMagma/lava crystallizesIgneous rock
    Weathering → Transportation → DepositionRock breaks down; particles move and settleSediment
    Lithification (Compaction + Cementation)Sediment grains compacted and cementedSedimentary rock
    Heat & Pressure (Metamorphism)Solid rock changes mineralogy/textureMetamorphic rock
    MeltingAny rock melts at sufficient temperatureMagma
    Uplift & ExposureDeep rocks brought to surface by erosionExposed to weathering
    🔄 No Rock Type is Permanent Granite (igneous) can be weathered into sand (sediment) → sandstone (sedimentary) → quartzite (metamorphic) → magma → granite again. The cycle operates over millions to billions of years and is fundamentally driven by Earth's internal heat (plate tectonics) and solar energy (driving surface weathering and erosion).

    Mineral Resources and Geologic Processes

    Economically valuable mineral deposits form through specific points in the rock cycle:

    • Chemical reactions with fluids — Hot hydrothermal fluids moving through rock precipitate ore minerals (gold, copper, lead).
    • Fractional crystallization — Minerals crystallize from magma at different temperatures, concentrating valuable metals (e.g., platinum-group elements in layered intrusions like the Stillwater Complex, Montana).
    • Erosion and concentration — Dense, resistant minerals (gold, diamonds) concentrate in river gravels as placer deposits.

    Mineral Identification Guide — 9 Common Minerals

    The following minerals are commonly encountered in Earth science fieldwork, laboratory specimens, and IESO/NEO practical tasks. Know them by sight and by property.

    Quartz Mineral
    SiO₂
    Hardness: 7 (Mohs) Luster: Vitreous (glassy) Color: Colorless, white, pink, purple (amethyst), smoke Diaphaneity: Transparent to translucent Cleavage: None (conchoidal fracture) Streak: White Notes: Most common mineral in continental crust; forms last in Bowen's series; abundant in granite and sandstone.
    K-Feldspar (Orthoclase) Mineral
    KAlSi₃O₈
    Hardness: 6 Luster: Vitreous to pearly Color: Pink, salmon, white, gray Diaphaneity: Translucent to opaque Cleavage: 2 directions at 90° Streak: White Notes: Most abundant mineral group on Earth; essential component of granite; forms by late-stage Bowen's crystallization.
    Muscovite Mica Mineral
    KAl₂(AlSi₃O₁₀)(OH)₂
    Hardness: 2–2.5 Luster: Pearly / vitreous Color: Colorless, silver, pale yellow Diaphaneity: Transparent to translucent Cleavage: 1 perfect cleavage (splits into thin flexible sheets) Streak: White Notes: Light-colored mica; found in granite, schist, pegmatite. Flexible, elastic sheets are diagnostic.
    Biotite Mica Mineral
    K(Mg,Fe)₃(AlSi₃O₁₀)(F,OH)₂
    Hardness: 2.5–3 Luster: Vitreous to pearly Color: Black, dark brown Diaphaneity: Opaque to translucent in thin sheets Cleavage: 1 perfect cleavage (flexible dark sheets) Streak: White to gray Notes: Dark mica; Fe-Mg content; found in granite, schist, gneiss. Forms in Bowen's series at medium T. Weathers to clay.
    Amphibole (Hornblende) Mineral
    Si₈O₂₂(OH)₂ + Ca,Fe,Mg,Na
    Hardness: 5–6 Luster: Vitreous Color: Dark green to black Diaphaneity: Opaque Cleavage: 2 at 60°/120° (diagnostic!) Streak: Gray-white Notes: Common in granite, diorite, amphibolite. Distinguish from pyroxene by cleavage angle: amphibole ≈ 60°, pyroxene ≈ 90°.
    Olivine Mineral
    (Mg,Fe)₂SiO₄
    Hardness: 6.5–7 Luster: Vitreous (glassy) Color: Olive green to yellow-green Diaphaneity: Transparent to translucent Cleavage: Poor; conchoidal fracture Streak: White Notes: First mineral to crystallize in Bowen's Series (highest T). Dominant in basalt, gabbro, and Earth's mantle (peridotite). Gem-quality = peridot.
    Calcite Mineral
    CaCO₃
    Hardness: 3 Luster: Vitreous to resinous Color: White, colorless, gray, yellow Diaphaneity: Transparent to translucent Cleavage: 3 directions (rhombohedral) Streak: White Notes: Main mineral of limestone and marble. Definitive test: fizzes vigorously in dilute HCl acid. Also forms stalactites and stalagmites.
    Halite (Rock Salt) Mineral
    NaCl
    Hardness: 2–2.5 Luster: Vitreous Color: Colorless, white, pink, blue Diaphaneity: Transparent Cleavage: 3 at 90° (perfect cubic) Streak: White Notes: Classic ionic bond example (Na⁺ + Cl⁻). Tastes salty. Forms as evaporite. Used in de-icing, food, and chemical industry.
    Hematite Mineral
    Fe₂O₃
    Hardness: 5.5–6.5 Luster: Metallic to earthy Color: Silver-gray (metallic), red-brown (earthy) Diaphaneity: Opaque Cleavage: None Streak: Red-brown (diagnostic!) Notes: Major iron ore mineral. Red color of many soils and sedimentary rocks is due to hematite coating. Common in banded iron formations (BIFs) — key marker of early Earth oxygenation.

    Rock Identification Guide

    Common Igneous Rocks Igneous

    Granite Igneous
    Origin: Plutonic (intrusive) Composition: Felsic (high silica) Texture: Phaneritic (coarse-grained, visible crystals) Minerals: Quartz + K-feldspar + plagioclase + biotite ± muscovite ± amphibole Color: Light gray, pink, white with black specks Environment: Continental crust; batholiths (e.g., Sierra Nevada) Uses: Construction, countertops, curbing
    Basalt Igneous
    Origin: Volcanic (extrusive) Composition: Mafic (low silica) Texture: Aphanitic (fine-grained, crystals not visible) Minerals: Plagioclase + pyroxene + olivine (microscopic) Color: Dark gray to black Environment: Oceanic crust; shield volcanoes; mid-ocean ridges (e.g., Hawaii) Uses: Road aggregate, fiber insulation
    Gabbro Igneous
    Origin: Plutonic (intrusive) Composition: Mafic Texture: Phaneritic (coarse-grained) Minerals: Plagioclase + pyroxene + olivine Color: Dark gray to black Environment: Oceanic crust (lower layer); layered intrusions Notes: Plutonic equivalent of basalt. Found in ophiolite sequences.
    Rhyolite Igneous
    Origin: Volcanic (extrusive) Composition: Felsic (high silica) Texture: Aphanitic; may show flow banding Minerals: Quartz + K-feldspar (microscopic) Color: Light gray, tan, pink, white Environment: Continental volcanic arcs; supervolcanoes Notes: Volcanic equivalent of granite. Very viscous lava → explosive eruptions.
    Obsidian Igneous
    Origin: Volcanic (extremely rapid cooling) Composition: Felsic Texture: Glassy (no crystals) Minerals: Natural volcanic glass (amorphous) Color: Black (sometimes brown or reddish) Environment: Lava flows, volcanic domes Notes: Conchoidal fracture produces razor-sharp edges; used by ancient peoples for tools and weapons.
    Pumice Igneous
    Origin: Volcanic (explosive, rapid) Composition: Felsic Texture: Vesicular (abundant tiny bubble holes) Color: White, gray, light tan Environment: Explosive silicic eruptions Notes: So porous it can float on water. Very low density. Used as abrasive, in concrete, and skincare.
    Scoria Igneous
    Origin: Volcanic Composition: Mafic Texture: Vesicular (scattered large vesicles) Color: Dark red, black, brown Environment: Basaltic lava flows, cinder cones Notes: Denser than pumice (mafic composition); sinks in water. Used in landscaping and drainage.

    Common Sedimentary Rocks Sedimentary

    Sandstone Sedimentary
    Type: Clastic Grain Size: Sand (0.06–2 mm) Composition: Mostly quartz; feldspar in arkose; rock fragments in lithic sandstone Color: Tan, red, brown, gray Environment: Beaches, river bars, desert dunes Notes: Good reservoir rock for oil and gas; aquifer rock for groundwater. Cross-bedding indicates paleocurrent direction.
    Shale Sedimentary
    Type: Clastic Grain Size: Clay + silt (<0.06 mm) Composition: Clay minerals, quartz Color: Dark gray, black, green, red Environment: Deep water, lakes, floodplains — quiet low-energy settings Notes: Most abundant sedimentary rock; cap rock for oil traps; splits along bedding planes (fissility). Source rock for petroleum.
    Limestone Sedimentary
    Type: Biochemical / Chemical Grain Size: Variable (fine to coarse) Composition: Calcite (CaCO₃) dominant Color: White, gray, tan, buff Environment: Warm shallow tropical seas (coral reefs, carbonate platforms) Notes: Fizzes in HCl. Often contains fossils. Basis of cement and lime. Dissolves to form karst topography (caves, sinkholes).
    Conglomerate Sedimentary
    Type: Clastic Grain Size: Gravel + (coarser, >2mm), rounded Composition: Rounded pebbles/cobbles cemented in sand or clay matrix Color: Variable — depends on clast types Environment: High-energy rivers, alluvial fans, beaches; grains rounded = transported far Notes: Rounded clasts = abrasion during transport. Angular equivalent = breccia (shorter transport or in-situ breakage).

    Common Metamorphic Rocks Metamorphic

    Marble Metamorphic
    Protolith: Limestone or dolostone Type: Non-foliated (contact or regional) Texture: Interlocking calcite/dolomite crystals; sugary to coarsely crystalline Color: White, pink, gray, green (with impurities) Grade: Low to medium Notes: Still fizzes in HCl (calcite present). Fossils destroyed by recrystallization. Used in sculpture and architecture (Michelangelo's David; Parthenon).
    Quartzite Metamorphic
    Protolith: Sandstone (quartz-rich) Type: Non-foliated Texture: Interlocking quartz crystals; very hard and tough Color: White, gray, pink, tan Grade: Low to high Notes: Hardness 7 (quartz). Unlike sandstone, breaks through (not around) grains. Extremely resistant to weathering → forms prominent ridges. Scratch test: quartzite breaks glassy; sandstone feels gritty and scratches easily.
    Schist Metamorphic
    Protolith: Shale / phyllite Type: Foliated (regional metamorphism) Texture: Coarse-grained; prominent schistosity (parallel mica sheets) Color: Silver-gray (muscovite schist), bronze-brown (biotite schist) Grade: Medium Notes: Garnet crystals often visible as red/purple porphyroblasts. Wavy, anastomosing foliation. Found in cores of mountain belts worldwide.

    In-Lecture Pop Quizzes & Concept Check

    🧪
    ConcepTest 1 — Porphyry Formation

    Geologists sometimes find a type of igneous rock known as porphyry, which contains both large and small crystals. Which is the best explanation for its formation?

    The rock experienced a two-stage cooling process...

    • A. Initial slow cooling at depth, then rapid cooling at surface
    • B. Initial rapid cooling at depth, then slow cooling at surface
    • C. Initial rapid cooling near surface, then slow cooling at depth
    • D. Initial slow cooling near surface, then rapid cooling at depth
    ▶ Reveal Answer & Explanation

    ✅ Answer: A — The large crystals (phenocrysts) grew slowly at depth in a magma chamber, forming visible crystals. The magma then erupted or moved upward, where rapid cooling prevented further large crystal growth, locking the large crystals inside a fine-grained (aphanitic) groundmass. This two-stage cooling history is preserved in the porphyritic texture. Key rule: large crystals = slow cooling; small crystals = fast cooling.

    🌊
    ConcepTest 2 — Sedimentary Process Steps

    Examine the diagram description below. Weathering, transportation, and deposition can occur during which steps of the rock cycle?

    Steps numbered 1–8 in a cycle diagram where: 1 = erosion of surface, 2 = stream transport, 3 = deposition at delta, 4 = burial and compaction, 5 = uplift of sedimentary rock, 6 = exposure at mountain top, 7 = glacial transport, 8 = ocean floor deposition.

    • A. Steps 1, 2, 3
    • B. Steps 3, 5, 7
    • C. Steps 2, 4, 8
    • D. Steps 4, 5, 6
    ▶ Reveal Answer & Explanation

    ✅ Answer: A (Steps 1, 2, 3) — Weathering occurs at step 1 (rock at surface breaks down), transportation at step 2 (sediment carried by stream), and deposition at step 3 (sediment drops where stream velocity decreases). Steps 4+ involve burial and lithification — different parts of the sedimentary cycle. This illustrates that weathering → transport → deposition is a tightly linked sequential process.

    💡
    Concept Q&A — Metamorphism Analogy

    The conversion of bread to toast can be seen as an analog for metamorphic rock formation. Which type does it best represent — Contact or Regional Metamorphism? Explain your reasoning.

    ▶ Reveal Answer & Explanation

    ✅ Answer: Contact Metamorphism. Toasting bread uses heat only from a nearby source (the toaster element), without any directional squeezing pressure. This directly parallels contact metamorphism, where rocks adjacent to a magma intrusion are "baked" by heat alone, producing non-foliated rocks like marble and quartzite. Regional metamorphism, in contrast, requires both elevated heat AND directional pressure (as in mountain building) — more analogous to pressing and heating clay simultaneously. The bread-to-toast analogy breaks down precisely where regional metamorphism differs: the toast doesn't develop foliation (parallel layers) because no pressure is applied directionally.

    🔬
    Mini Quiz — Silicate Identification

    Which of the following mineral formulas represents a silicate mineral? (Silica tes contain both Si and O in the formula.)

    • A. FeS₂ (iron sulfide)
    • B. KAlSi₃O₈ (potassium, aluminum silicate)
    • C. Fe₂O₃ (iron oxide)
    • D. CaSO₄·2H₂O (calcium sulfate)
    ▶ Reveal Answer & Explanation

    ✅ Answer: B — KAlSi₃O₈ (Orthoclase Feldspar). The defining feature of silicate minerals is the presence of silicon (Si) bonded to oxygen (O), forming the SiO₄ tetrahedron unit. Option B contains Si₃O₈, clearly a silicate framework. Option A is a sulfide (FeS₂ = pyrite), C is an oxide (Fe₂O₃ = hematite), and D is a sulfate (gypsum). Silicates are the dominant mineral group in Earth's crust precisely because Si and O are the two most abundant crustal elements.

    Glossary of Key Terms

    Atom
    Smallest particle retaining the chemical properties of an element. Contains protons, neutrons, and electrons.
    Ion
    Atom that has gained or lost electrons, acquiring a positive (cation) or negative (anion) electric charge.
    Ionic Bond
    Chemical bond formed by electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (e.g., Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in halite).
    Covalent Bond
    Chemical bond formed by sharing electrons between atoms; generally stronger than ionic bonds.
    Silica Tetrahedron
    Basic structural unit of silicate minerals: one Si atom bonded to 4 oxygen atoms (SiO₄), forming a tetrahedron.
    Mineral
    Naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and ordered internal atomic structure.
    Cleavage
    The tendency of a mineral to break along flat, smooth planes reflecting weaker atomic bonds.
    Hardness (Mohs)
    Relative scale of a mineral's resistance to scratching (1 = talc, 10 = diamond).
    Luster
    Quality of light reflected from a mineral surface — metallic vs. non-metallic (vitreous, pearly, silky, etc.).
    Streak
    Color of a mineral's powder when scratched on unglazed porcelain; more consistent than surface color.
    Magma
    Molten rock below Earth's surface, including dissolved gases and some solid material.
    Lava
    Magma that has reached Earth's surface through a volcanic eruption.
    Igneous Rock
    Rock formed by cooling and solidification of magma or lava.
    Plutonic Rock
    Igneous rock that forms deep underground by slow cooling → coarse-grained texture.
    Volcanic Rock
    Igneous rock that forms at or near Earth's surface by rapid cooling → fine-grained or glassy texture.
    Aphanitic
    Fine-grained igneous texture; crystals too small to see without magnification.
    Phaneritic
    Coarse-grained igneous texture; crystals visible to naked eye (>0.5 mm).
    Porphyritic
    Igneous texture with two crystal size populations (phenocrysts in fine groundmass), indicating two-stage cooling.
    Felsic
    Silica-rich (high SiO₂) igneous rock composition; typically light-colored; contains quartz and feldspar.
    Mafic
    Silica-poor igneous rock composition; dark-colored; rich in Mg and Fe minerals (amphibole, pyroxene, olivine).
    Bowen's Reaction Series
    Sequence in which silicate minerals crystallize from cooling magma, from olivine (highest T) to quartz (lowest T).
    Sediment
    Fragments of rock and mineral particles produced by weathering and erosion, classified by grain size.
    Lithification
    Process converting sediment into sedimentary rock through compaction and cementation.
    Clastic Rock
    Sedimentary rock composed of fragments of pre-existing rock and minerals.
    Evaporite
    Chemical sedimentary rock formed by precipitation of minerals from evaporating water (e.g., halite, gypsum).
    Metamorphism
    Solid-state changes in mineralogy and/or texture due to elevated T and/or P, without melting.
    Protolith
    The original (parent) rock before metamorphism occurred.
    Foliation
    Planar alignment of minerals in metamorphic rocks, produced by directional pressure during regional metamorphism.
    Contact Metamorphism
    Heat-driven metamorphism near igneous intrusions; typically produces non-foliated rocks over a small zone.
    Regional Metamorphism
    Heat + pressure metamorphism associated with plate tectonics and mountain building; produces foliated rocks over large areas.
    Rock Cycle
    Continuous set of processes by which rocks of any type are transformed into rocks of any other type over geological time.
    Neptunism
    Early (incorrect) hypothesis that all rocks formed from precipitation or settling in a global ocean.
    Plutonism
    Hutton's correct hypothesis that Earth's internal heat drives rock formation through melting and cooling.
    Placer Deposit
    Concentration of dense, resistant minerals (gold, diamonds) in river gravels through erosional sorting.
